Many dispensational and other evangelical writers; the theme of the 'Laodicean' end-time church (Revelation 3:14–22) in dispensational church-age schemes.

Paul says the day of the Lord will not come unless the apostasy comes first, and warns that in the last days people will have a form of godliness but deny its power (2 Timothy 3:5) and will not endure sound teaching (4:3–4). The marked decline of historic Christianity in Europe and North America, and the abandonment of biblical doctrine in some denominations, fits these warnings.

Paul tells Timothy to 'avoid such people' (2 Timothy 3:5), showing that the 'last days' were already present in Timothy's time, and 1 John 2:18 says 'it is the last hour' because many antichrists had already come. Every generation since has seen apostasy. Globally, Christianity has grown dramatically in Africa, Asia and Latin America during the same decades in which Western churches declined, so the world church looks very different from a single falling away. Postmillennialists in particular argue that the gospel is advancing, not retreating. Some critics also observe that the theme can be used to dismiss other Christians rather than to examine oneself.

Dispensationalists answer that the climactic apostasy of 2 Thessalonians 2 is future and connected with the man of lawlessness, while present apostasy is a trend consistent with it; some (for example H. Wayne House and Andy Woods) argue that apostasia here means 'departure', the rapture itself, which would make the verse a sign of a different kind. They acknowledge global church growth and see the Laodicean picture as a warning to every church rather than a timetable.

Doctrinal and moral drift is a real concern recognised across traditions, and the New Testament warns of it. But the 'last days' language of the epistles already applied to the first century, apostasy has accompanied every age, and the global growth of the church complicates any claim that the great falling away is now. The text is most fruitfully read as a call to self-examination and faithfulness.
Damascus a heap of ruins (Isaiah 17)
2011 to the present

Isaiah 17:1 ('Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins') awaits fulfilment, and the Syrian civil war from 2011, Israeli strikes in Syria and the fall of the Assad government in December 2024 point towards it.
Popular prophecy writers and broadcasters, including some who link it with Psalm 83 and Ezekiel 38.

Damascus claims to be among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, so it has never been a 'heap of ruins' as Isaiah describes. The prophecy must therefore be future, and the long Syrian conflict and Israeli–Syrian hostility make its destruction conceivable.

Isaiah 17 is an oracle against the eighth-century BC alliance of Damascus (Aram) and Ephraim (the northern kingdom of Israel), whom it names together (17:3). Assyria under Tiglath-pileser III captured Damascus in 732 BC, deported its people and killed its king Rezin (2 Kings 16:9), and Samaria fell in 722 BC; the prophecy was fulfilled as Isaiah's first readers would have understood it, with the hyperbolic language typical of oracles against nations. Damascus being later rebuilt no more falsifies the prophecy than Jerusalem's rebuilding falsified prophecies of its destruction. Despite years of war, Damascus has not been destroyed, and specific predictions of its imminent destruction have repeatedly passed.

Some dispensational writers accept the 732 BC fulfilment, at least in part; others argue for a double fulfilment, with a final destruction still to come, while generally avoiding dates. Many caution against reading Isaiah 17 into each development in the Syrian conflict.

The contextual case for a fulfilment in 732 BC is strong, and many futurists accept it; a future second fulfilment is possible on some futurist principles but is not required by the text. Predictions linking the Syrian war to Isaiah 17 have so far failed, and such claims are especially sensitive given the human cost of that war.
1. Crisis

The cycle almost always begins with a real crisis: persecution in Thessalonica, plague in Gregory's Rome and in 1348, the Turkish advance, revolution in France, the Cold War, war in the Gulf, a pandemic. Crises make the world feel unstable and the present feel decisive. Psychologists describe a recency bias in which the events we live through feel uniquely important; in fact every generation since the apostles has had its own crises, and the New Testament already said 'it is the last hour' (1 John 2:18), meaning that the whole age between Christ's comings is the last days.
2. Newspaper exegesis

Readers then interpret Scripture through the news, rather than the news through Scripture: a current power is fitted to Gog, a leader to Antichrist, a technology to the mark. Humans are pattern-seeking creatures, and apophenia, the tendency to see meaningful connections in random data, is strengthened by confirmation bias, which notices matches and overlooks misfits. The original audience and context of a prophecy fade, and its symbols become a code for the reader's own headlines.
3. Identification and date

The identification becomes a timeline and often a date, either explicitly (Miller, Whisenant, Camping) or by implication (1948 plus a generation). Numbers carry special persuasive force because they feel objective; round numbers and anniversaries (1000, 1260, 1666, 2000, 1948 + 70) attract particular attention. Many date-setters hedge, but hearers remember the date and forget the hedge.
4. Mobilisation

The expectation produces action: books and broadcasts, revival meetings, sales of property, withdrawal from work (as in Thessalonica), flight to mountains or refuges, sometimes violence (the Taborites, Münster) or support for political causes. Some of this energy is genuinely good, such as mission, generosity and repentance; some is harmful, especially when the end is to be brought about by force or when scapegoats are blamed.
5. Disappointment

The date passes or the identification collapses: the emperor dies, the pope recovers, the Common Market grows to twelve, the eclipse comes and goes. Disappointment can destroy faith, as in many Millerites in 1844 and Jehovah's Witnesses after 1975, and it gives sceptics an argument against Christian hope itself (2 Peter 3:3–4).
6. Reinterpretation or a new date

Studies of failed prophecy, beginning with the 1956 study of a small UFO group in 'When Prophecy Fails', show that committed groups often respond to disconfirmation not by abandoning belief but by reinterpreting it: the event happened invisibly or in heaven (1844, 1914), the calculation was slightly wrong (Cotton Mather, Camping, Whisenant), or the sign was only a forerunner. Sometimes, though, there is real repentance: Family Radio's 2012 apology and the Worldwide Church of God's reformation show that the cycle can be broken.
7. Breaking the cycle

Theologically, the cycle is broken by recovering three truths held across the millennial views: the 'last days' began with Christ (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2), so every generation lives in them; Jesus forbade knowledge of the day and hour while commanding constant readiness (Matthew 24:36–44); and the signs he gave were meant to keep disciples faithful and unshaken, not to enable calculation (Matthew 24:6). Augustine's refusal to calculate the end, the warnings of Hippolytus, and modern dispensational scholars' rejection of date-setting all point the same way.
No one knows the day or hour

Jesus said that no one knows the day or the hour, not even the angels nor the Son in his earthly ministry, but the Father only. Arguments that we may know the year or season but not the day misread the point, which is that the timing is hidden and the disciple's task is readiness.
Times and seasons belong to the Father

When the disciples asked whether Jesus would now restore the kingdom to Israel, he did not deny a future restoration but said the times and seasons were not theirs to know; their task was to be witnesses in the power of the Spirit. The question of timing is redirected to mission.
Failed predictions are a test

Deuteronomy says that when a prophet speaks in the Lord's name and the word does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it. A teacher who announces a date or event as certain and is proved wrong should be heard with caution, not simply allowed to set a new date; at the same time, an interpreter who offers a tentative suggestion, clearly marked as such, is not a false prophet.
Not surprised, because always ready

Paul says the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night, but believers are not in darkness so that it surprises them. The reason they are not surprised is not that they have calculated the date but that they are awake and sober, living as children of the day.
God's time and God's patience

Peter answers scoffers who say 'Where is the promise of his coming?' by reminding them that with the Lord a day is as a thousand years, and that the delay is God's patience, not wishing any to perish. The verse is about God's perspective on time, not a code for calculation (as Hippolytus and later chronologers used it).
Watch by working

Mark's version of the Olivet Discourse ends with a man going on a journey who gives each servant his work and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake. Watchfulness in the New Testament means faithful work, prayer and holiness, not scanning the headlines.
The text meant something to its first readers

Revelation was written to seven real churches who were told it was 'soon' and 'near' and were blessed for keeping it (Revelation 1:3; 22:10). Whatever future fulfilment one expects, an interpretation that would have meant nothing to them (barcodes, the EU, AI) should be treated with great caution. All the main views, including futurist ones, agree that the first readers needed and received its message.
Respect the genre of prophecy

Prophetic and apocalyptic texts use symbols, numbers and cosmic imagery drawn from the Old Testament, and they often describe God's judgments in hyperbolic language (compare Isaiah 13:10 on Babylon). They are written to reveal God's rule and call for faithfulness; they are not encrypted newspapers. Interpreters across the millennial views differ on how literally to read them, but all should begin with how the imagery works in Scripture before asking what it might correspond to today.

Jesus did not only forbid date-setting; he commanded his followers to watch, to learn the lesson of the fig tree, and to lift up their heads when 'these things begin to take place' (Luke 21:28), and he rebuked those who could read the sky but not the signs of the times (Matthew 16:3). Proponents argue that it would be strange to obey the first command and ignore the second, and that reading the world in the light of Scripture is simply faithful discipleship. They point out that the return of the Jewish people to their land after nearly two thousand years, against all historical odds and contrary to the expectations of many interpreters who had spiritualised those prophecies, is at least a striking event that a believing reader of Ezekiel and Romans 11 should not shrug off. Many of the most serious futurist scholars, such as John Walvoord, J. Dwight Pentecost and Thomas Ice, have consistently rejected date-setting, criticised Whisenant, Camping and the blood-moons teachers, and taught that the rapture is imminent and signless, so that present events can only be stage-setting. On this view, the failures of popular date-setters no more discredit watchfulness than counterfeit money discredits real currency, and critics who lump scholars and sensationalists together are being unfair. Proponents add that many great revivals and missionary movements were fuelled by a lively expectation of Christ's return, and that a church which no longer expects him soon tends to grow comfortable. Finally, they note that every generation has to live as if it might be the last, because one generation will be, and the believers alive then are told they will see the signs and recognise them.

When was Revelation written: in the 60s, while Nero ruled and the Jerusalem temple still stood, or around 95, near the end of Domitian's reign, a generation after the temple fell? The question sounds technical, but it shapes how the whole book can be read. If John wrote before AD 70, the judgments on 'the great city' and the trampling of the holy city could be prophecies of the Jewish War and the fall of Jerusalem, as partial and full preterists hold. If he wrote after 70, those events were already past, and the book's warnings must point to Rome, to the course of history, or to the end of the age. Both sides appeal to ancient testimony (what the early church remembered) and to internal evidence (what the book itself seems to presuppose), and both have serious scholars behind them. This study sets out each side's strongest evidence, with the best reply to each, so you can weigh it for yourself.
Before AD 70
c. AD 64-69, under Nero (54-68) or during the brief reign of Galba (68-69)

On this view John received his visions during or just after Nero's persecution of Christians in Rome (from AD 64) and before the Romans destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in August 70. Its advocates rest mainly on internal evidence: the temple and altar are measured as though still standing (11:1-2), the sixth of seven kings 'is' now reigning (17:10), the number 666 spells Nero Caesar in Hebrew letters, and the book insists its events are near. They argue that the external testimony for Domitian rests largely on one ambiguous sentence of Irenaeus, and they point to scattered ancient traditions placing John's exile under Nero. They also find it hard to believe that a book so full of temple imagery and judgment would never mention the greatest judgment of the age if it had already happened.
Under Domitian
c. AD 95-96, near the end of Domitian's reign (81-96)

On this view John was banished to Patmos under Domitian and wrote around 95, about twenty-five years after Jerusalem fell. Its advocates rest first on external evidence: Irenaeus, who knew Polycarp, a disciple of John, says the vision was seen 'towards the end of Domitian's reign', and Victorinus, Eusebius and Jerome agree. They add internal evidence: the seven churches seem to have a history of decline, Laodicea boasts of a wealth that suits its recovery after the earthquake of 60, Rome is called 'Babylon' as Jewish writers did only after 70, and the imperial cult and a myth of Nero's return fit the Flavian period. They answer the early-date texts by reading the temple of chapter 11 as a visionary symbol and the seven kings and 666 as open to several counts.
Irenaeus: the vision was seen towards the end of Domitian's reign

Irenaeus of Lyons, writing about 180, declines to name the Antichrist from the number 666, reasoning that if the name were needed it would have been announced by the one who saw the apocalypse, 'for it was seen not very long ago, but almost in our own generation, towards the end of Domitian's reign.' Irenaeus grew up in Asia and heard Polycarp of Smyrna, who had known John, so this is the earliest explicit date and comes through a short chain of Asian memory. Eusebius quotes the Greek twice and plainly took it to date the vision. Late-date advocates regard it as the single strongest piece of evidence: early, specific and from a writer with direct links to the region.

The verb heōrathē ('was seen') has no expressed subject, and the nearest personal antecedent is John, 'the one who saw the apocalypse', so early-date advocates argue it may mean that John himself was seen, that is, was still alive and accessible, under Domitian; Irenaeus elsewhere stresses that John lived on into Trajan's reign (2.22.5; 3.3.4). They also note Irenaeus' chronological slips, such as his claim that Jesus' ministry continued until he was over forty (2.22.5-6). On this view one ambiguous sentence from a writer a century later should not outweigh the book's own internal signals.
Victorinus: condemned to the mines of Patmos by Domitian

Victorinus of Pettau (died c. 304), author of the oldest surviving Latin commentary on Revelation, says that when John saw the visions he was on Patmos, condemned to labour in the mines by Caesar Domitian, and that after Domitian's death, when his decrees were annulled, John was released and afterwards published the Apocalypse. On 17:10 he identifies the king who 'is' with Domitian. Late-date advocates value this as a western witness that adds concrete detail, penal labour, rather than merely repeating Irenaeus' words.

Victorinus may simply depend on Irenaeus, and his commentary contains other historical confusions. To make Domitian the king who 'is' in 17:10 he has to begin counting after Nero, from Galba, so that Nero can return as the eighth king, a count early-date advocates regard as arbitrary. No other early source mentions mines on Patmos, so the detail may be an embellishment of the general tradition of exile.
Clement of Alexandria: John returned 'after the tyrant's death'

Clement of Alexandria, about 200, says that 'after the tyrant's death' John returned from the island of Patmos to Ephesus, where he travelled about the region appointing bishops, and then tells the story of the aged apostle reclaiming a young man who had become a robber chief. Eusebius quotes the whole passage in his account of Domitian's reign and its aftermath, taking the tyrant to be Domitian. Late-date advocates note that Clement calls John an old man and that 'tyrant' matches how Christian writers remembered Domitian, so Clement fits the same picture as Irenaeus.

Clement does not name the tyrant, and in Christian memory Nero was the tyrant par excellence, the first emperor to persecute the church; the identification with Domitian is Eusebius'. Early-date advocates add that the story has John mounting a horse and riding hard after the robber, which suits a man of about sixty in the late 60s better than one near ninety after 96. Gentry also notes that Clement elsewhere says the teaching of the apostles ended with Paul's ministry under Nero (Miscellanies 7.17).
Origen: 'the king of the Romans, as tradition teaches'

Origen, commenting on Jesus' word that James and John would drink his cup, writes that 'the king of the Romans, as tradition teaches, condemned John, who bore witness on account of the word of truth, to the island of Patmos', and that John himself tells of this in the Apocalypse without naming who condemned him. Late-date advocates read 'tradition' as the same Domitianic tradition already known from Irenaeus and Clement, so Origen adds a third-century Alexandrian voice to a consistent picture of exile by imperial sentence.

Origen pointedly leaves the emperor unnamed, and his wording fits Nero just as well as Domitian, so neither side can claim him with confidence. His remark that Revelation itself does not name the king shows only that the book is silent on the point. A witness that leaves the key detail blank adds little to the case beyond confirming that John was exiled by a Roman ruler.
Eusebius: banished under Domitian, released under Nerva, alive under Trajan

Eusebius places John's banishment to Patmos in Domitian's persecution and quotes Irenaeus in support (Church History 3.18.1-3). He says that after Domitian's death the senate annulled his decrees and the exiles came home, so that 'the ancient tradition of the Christians' records John's return from Patmos to Ephesus (3.20.8-9). He adds that John lived on in Asia into Trajan's reign, citing Irenaeus and Clement (3.23.1-4). Eusebius worked with the large library at Caesarea, including sources now lost, and late-date advocates see his account as the settled memory of the early church.

Eusebius explicitly builds on Irenaeus and Clement, so he multiplies citations rather than independent witnesses: if Irenaeus was misread, Eusebius inherits the misreading. Early-date writers also point out that in his Demonstration of the Gospel (3.5) Eusebius mentions John's banishment in the same breath as the deaths of Peter and Paul under Nero, which some read as reflecting a Neronian setting. Eusebius was also openly uncertain about Revelation's authorship and standing (3.25; 7.25), so his chronology of it may not have been closely examined.
Jerome: banished in Domitian's fourteenth year

Jerome says that in the fourteenth year of Domitian (about 94-95) John was banished to the island of Patmos and wrote the Apocalypse there, and that after Domitian's death, when the senate annulled his acts, John returned to Ephesus under Nerva. Jerome was the most learned Latin scholar of his age, had travelled widely in the East, and gives the most precise date in the tradition. Late-date advocates see his testimony as confirming that by the late fourth century the Domitianic date was the standard view in both East and West.

Jerome wrote three centuries after the event and is visibly dependent on Eusebius, so he adds precision rather than independent evidence. In another work he reports Tertullian's story of John being cast into boiling oil at Rome and says that it was Nero who did it (Against Jovinian 1.26), which suggests the traditions about John's sufferings were less fixed than On Illustrious Men implies. Early-date advocates argue that late, derivative witnesses cannot strengthen a tradition beyond its first source.
Ephesus has left its first love, and Paul is not mentioned

The letter to Ephesus describes a church that has long endured, has tested and rejected false apostles, and yet 'has abandoned the love you had at first' (2:2-4). Paul founded this church around 52, spent nearly three years there and wrote to it (or to its region) around 60-62, praising its love for all the saints (Ephesians 1:15). Late-date advocates argue that a decline from that first love, in a church now addressed without any mention of Paul or Timothy, fits a second generation after Paul's death better than a few years after his letter. Mark Wilson argues that the history of the Ephesian church, with John as its later leading figure, points to the 90s.

Churches can decline quickly: Paul marvelled that the Galatians were 'so quickly deserting' the gospel within a few years (Galatians 1:6). He warned the Ephesian elders around 57 that fierce wolves would come and that men would arise among them speaking twisted things (Acts 20:29-30), and the letters to Timothy, traditionally dated to the mid-60s, already show false teachers and defections at Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:3-7; 2 Timothy 1:15). By 65 the church was more than a decade old, enough time for a first love to cool.
The seven churches seem to have a history

Several of the churches look settled and past their beginnings. Sardis has 'a reputation of being alive, but you are dead' (3:1); Laodicea has become lukewarm (3:15-16); 'Jezebel' at Thyatira has been given 'time to repent' and her followers have learned 'the deep things of Satan' (2:20-24); and Antipas at Pergamum was killed some time before (2:13). Late-date advocates argue that this picture of established congregations, internal factions and spiritual decline suits churches a generation or more after their founding in the 50s, and that the letters show no awareness of Paul's recent ministry in the province.

Paul's own letters show similar problems arising within a few years of a church's founding: factions, immorality and food offered to idols at Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:11-12; 5:1; 8-10) and dangerous teaching at nearby Colossae around 60 (Colossians 2:8-23). Colossians even warns Archippus, apparently connected with the Lycus valley churches including Laodicea, to fulfil his ministry (Colossians 4:16-17). The churches of Asia had existed for roughly fifteen years by 65, long enough for reputations to rise and fall.
Laodicea's boast of wealth after the earthquake of AD 60

Tacitus records that in AD 60 Laodicea, one of the famous cities of Asia, was laid in ruins by an earthquake and 'recovered by its own resources, without help from us' (Annals 14.27). The church echoes the city's pride: 'I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing' (3:17). Late-date advocates, following Colin Hemer, argue that rebuilding a major city took decades, with major public buildings still being completed and dedicated in the following decades, so a boast of flourishing wealth suits the 90s better than a few years after the disaster.

Tacitus' point is precisely that Laodicea was rich enough in 60 to refuse imperial help, so its proud self-sufficiency predates the earthquake and would be an apt target in the mid-60s. The boast in 3:17 is the church's spiritual complacency, not a description of a completed building programme, and Christ answers it with spiritual remedies (gold refined by fire, white garments, eye salve). A city that could rebuild without aid was by definition already wealthy.
Did a church at Smyrna exist in the 60s?

Revelation addresses an established church at Smyrna that has known tribulation, poverty and slander (2:8-11). Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, tells the Philippians that Paul boasted of them 'in all the churches which alone then knew the Lord, for we had not yet known him' (11.3). Late-date advocates read this to mean that the church at Smyrna did not yet exist while Paul was writing, so an established Smyrnaean church with a history of suffering points well after the 60s.

Polycarp's 'then' most naturally refers to the time when the Philippians first believed and Paul first praised them (around 50), not to the 60s. Acts says that during Paul's Ephesian ministry (about 52-55) 'all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord' (Acts 19:10), which makes a church at Smyrna by the mid-50s likely. The passage survives only in a Latin translation, and its 'we' may refer to Polycarp's own generation rather than the Smyrnaean church as such.
'Babylon' as a name for Rome appears in Jewish writings after 70

Revelation calls the great city 'Babylon the great' (14:8; 17:5; 18:2). In Jewish literature this code name for Rome appears in works written after 70, when Rome, like Babylon in 587 BC, had destroyed Jerusalem and its temple: 4 Ezra opens 'in the thirtieth year after the destruction of the city' with the seer 'in Babylon' (3:1-2), and 2 Baruch and the fifth Sibylline Oracle use the name the same way. Late-date advocates argue that the name presupposes the second temple's destruction and so requires a date after 70.

1 Peter already calls Rome 'Babylon' (5:13), and early-date advocates hold that 1 Peter was written before Peter's death under Nero, though many critical scholars date it later. Babylon was a natural symbol of proud pagan power and of God's people in exile without any reference to the temple's fall (Isaiah 13-14; 47; Jeremiah 50-51). Many partial preterists in any case identify Babylon in Revelation with apostate Jerusalem, 'the great city where their Lord was crucified' (11:8), which removes the argument entirely.
The legend of Nero's return needed time to grow

The beast has a mortal wound that is healed (13:3, 12, 14); it 'was, and is not, and is about to rise from the abyss', and is 'an eighth, but belongs to the seven' (17:8, 11). Many scholars see behind this the legend that Nero had not really died or would return from the east. Pretenders appeared in 69 (Tacitus, Histories 2.8), under Titus (Dio 66.19) and about twenty years after Nero's death (Suetonius, Nero 57), and the returning Nero is developed in Sibylline Oracles 4.119-39 (about 80) and book 5. Late-date advocates argue that a myth that had to grow and then be reimagined as a return from the abyss points to the Flavian period, most naturally Domitian, whom the satirist Juvenal called a 'bald Nero' (Satires 4.38).

Tacitus shows the rumour active in Achaia and Asia in 69, within a year of Nero's death, and Suetonius says some at once refused to believe he was dead, so the legend does not require a late date to be known. Early-date advocates such as Gentry further deny that Revelation uses the legend at all: they read the healed wound as the Roman empire's near-collapse in the civil wars of 68-69 and its recovery under Vespasian, and the beast that 'was, is not, and is to come' as a parody of God's name in 1:4. If John is turning a rumour inside out, he could do so whenever it circulated.
Emperor worship under Domitian: 'our lord and god' and the Ephesian temple

Revelation 13 depicts a second beast that compels worship of the first beast and its image and controls buying and selling (13:11-17). Under Domitian the imperial cult in Asia reached a new pitch: a provincial temple of the Sebastoi (the Flavian emperors), with a colossal statue, was dedicated at Ephesus around 89-90, and Suetonius says Domitian had official letters begin 'Our Lord and God commands', so that the title became customary (Domitian 13). Late-date advocates see this as the most fitting setting for a book about refusing to worship the beast and its image.

Emperor worship was established in Asia long before Domitian, with provincial temples to Augustus and Roma at Pergamum (29 BC) and to Tiberius at Smyrna (AD 26); Caligula ordered his statue set up in the Jerusalem temple (AD 40), and Nero was honoured in divine terms, with a proposal in the senate to build him a temple as a god (Tacitus, Annals 15.74). Leonard Thompson and Steven Friesen argue that the hostile 'lord and god' portrait comes from writers after Domitian's death who wished to blacken him, and that the imperial cult was civic and pervasive throughout the century rather than a Domitianic novelty. So the cult fits either date.
Persecution and banishment under Domitian

Christian writers from Melito of Sardis (about 170, quoted by Eusebius 4.26.9) onward name Domitian, alongside Nero, as a persecutor. Dio Cassius records that in 95 Domitian executed his cousin, the consul Flavius Clemens, and banished his wife Flavia Domitilla on a charge of 'atheism', for which many others 'who drifted into Jewish ways' were condemned (67.14); Eusebius says a Domitilla was banished for her testimony to Christ (3.18.4). 1 Clement, usually dated about 95-96, apologises for delay due to 'sudden and repeated misfortunes' at Rome (1.1). Late-date advocates find here the pressure behind Revelation's martyrs (2:13; 6:9-11) and John's own exile 'on account of the word of God' (1:9).
